opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think perfectionism played a real role, though it's tangled up with some things that I'd defend as legitimate. Grantmaking in technical AI safety is a domain where the quality of judgment really matters. A lot of the value comes from the distinctions: is this research agenda actually going to tell us something about whether models are scheming, or is it something that looks safety-flavored but won't move the needle? Those calls are hard, and I felt like I'd built up a particular model of what mattered over years of thinking about timelines and alignment risk.

So when I tried to hand work off, I'd find myself wanting the other person to reach the same conclusions I would, for the same reasons, written up the way I would write them. That's a pretty unreasonable bar. Part of the point of growing a team is that other people bring different views, and sometimes they'll be right where I'm wrong. If I insist on reviewing everything at the level of "would I have written this sentence," I've basically just created a bottleneck with extra steps.

The other piece is that perfectionism made the cost of my own time feel invisible. I'd think, "it'll be faster if I just do this myself," and on any individual grant that was often true. But summed over a year, it meant we funded less, moved slower, and the field was supply-constrained on exactly the kind of work we wanted more of. Being a bit worse on each decision but making many more decisions was probably the better trade, and I didn't fully internalize that.

What I've tried to shift toward is being clearer about which decisions actually need my judgment, like big strategic bets or areas where I have unusual context, and then letting go on the rest, accepting that "good and fast" beats "perfect and late" in a field that's moving as quickly as AI is. It's still something I'm working on, honestly.

r001.rationale: Cotra says she wanted delegated work to match her conclusions and writing, and that reviewing everything to that standard created a bottleneck; she also says doing each grant herself often felt faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think perfectionism was a huge part of it, maybe the biggest part. When I was doing grantmaking at Open Phil, I had this very specific, very detailed picture in my head of what a good grant looked like, what a good reasoning process looked like, what the writeup should say. And when I would try to hand something off, I'd look at what came back and I'd see all the ways it diverged from what I would have done. And my instinct was always to treat those divergences as errors rather than as just, you know, different reasonable choices.

So what would happen is I'd either take the work back and redo it myself, which obviously defeats the purpose of delegating, or I'd give so much feedback that the person on the other end felt micromanaged and demoralized. Neither of those is a good outcome. And the thing is, in a lot of cases, if I'm honest, the difference between my version and their version wasn't actually going to change whether we funded the thing or how much. I was optimizing for a kind of polish that didn't cash out in better decisions.

I think there was also an identity component. A lot of my sense of being good at the job was tied up in the details, in being the person who had thought through every angle. And delegating means accepting that the output will have someone else's fingerprints on it, and that you'll be accountable for something you didn't fully shape. That was uncomfortable for me in a way I didn't fully recognize at the time. I'd tell myself it was about quality, but some of it was about control, and about not wanting to be in a position where I couldn't defend every sentence.

The thing that eventually helped was reframing what the actual bottleneck was. In AI safety grantmaking, the scarce resource was never the perfect memo. It was throughput, it was getting money out the door to people who could use it, it was my own attention being freed up for the judgment calls that genuinely needed me. Once I started thinking about it as, what's the cost of this grant going out two months later because I insisted on rewriting it, the calculus looked really different. A B-plus decision made now is often worth more than an A decision made next quarter.

I'd also say I got better at distinguishing between the kinds of things where my taste actually mattered and the kinds where it didn't. There were a handful of judgment calls, like how to think about a particular researcher's track record, or whether a research direction was promising, where I think my view really did add something. But a lot of the rest was just execution, and other people could execute fine. Learning to spend my perfectionism only on the high-leverage stuff, rather than spreading it over everything, was probably the single most useful adjustment I made. I'm still not great at it, to be clear. But I'm at least aware of the pattern now, which is more than I could say for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response says Cotra would redo delegated work herself or give extensive feedback, and that insisting on rewriting could delay a grant. It does not say that revising the delegated work to meet her standards took longer than doing it herself from the start.

astra-6.text:
I think perfectionism is part of it. With grantmaking, you’re making consequential decisions under a lot of uncertainty, and there’s always another question you could ask or another consideration you could investigate. It’s hard to identify the point where you’ve done enough.

That makes delegation difficult because you have to let someone else exercise judgment. If I feel like I need to reconstruct their entire reasoning and become independently convinced of every step, then I haven’t really delegated very much. I’ve added another person to the process while keeping myself as the bottleneck.

I think the distinction I need to make is between having high standards for the work and needing the work to be done exactly the way I would do it. Those aren’t the same thing. Someone can notice different things, weigh considerations differently, and still make a good decision. Part of getting better at delegation is becoming comfortable with that, rather than treating every difference as something I need to resolve.

r001.rationale: The response says that needing to reconstruct and independently validate another person’s reasoning keeps Cotra as the bottleneck, but it does not say that revising their work to meet her standards takes longer than doing it herself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think perfectionism is part of it, but it shows up less as, “I need every detail to be perfect,” and more as, “I need to understand and endorse the reasoning behind this decision.” With grantmaking, there often isn’t a clear answer you can check against. You’re making a judgment under a lot of uncertainty, and two thoughtful people can come to different conclusions.

So if I delegate something and then feel like I need to reconstruct all the reasoning myself before I’m comfortable acting on it, I haven’t actually delegated very much. I’ve asked someone to do work, but I’m still holding on to the judgment.

The thing I need to get better at is distinguishing between, “This person is making a mistake,” and, “This person is approaching the question differently than I would.” You can have a process you trust without every decision being exactly the decision you would have made. But accepting that means being willing to feel some discomfort, rather than treating that discomfort as evidence that I need to take the work back.

r001.rationale: The response says Cotra may reconstruct the reasoning behind a delegated decision, but it does not say she revises delegated work to meet her standards or that doing so takes longer than doing the work herself.
